design_detail: Single-arm pretest–posttest pilot (the Fentanyl Innovative Testing, FIT, study), filed as a prospective cohort, nested in the EMERALD cohort of street-based cis-gender women who sell or trade sex in Baltimore, Maryland. 103 women who had used illegally obtained opioids in the past month were enrolled April 2018 to February 2019; at baseline all received a brief strip training, harm-reduction counselling tailored to their reported risks, an insert card, five fentanyl test strips (BTNX), injection equipment and naloxone, and were re-interviewed after a target of one month (mean 56 days). Outcomes: self-reported strip use, results and actions after results, acceptability, and pre–post changes in drug use, solitary use and overdose by McNemar's test, overall and stratified by strip use. Read from the PubMed Central author manuscript; 'AM p.' is the PDF page. Appraised with ROBINS-I, as for sc_krieger_2018, because strip provision with training is an intervention and the paper infers its effects.
can_establish: How many women in this Baltimore sample of women who sell sex and use opioids used the five strips within about two months, what results they reported, what they said they did after positive and negative results, and how acceptable they found the strips.
cannot_establish: Whether the strips, or the bundle of strips, counselling and naloxone, reduced drug use, solitary use or overdose: there was no comparison group, the women who used no strip changed as much or more, the baseline and follow-up questions on drug use covered different periods, and all outcomes were self-reported to study staff.

sample.recruitment: Targeted sampling with a mobile van in Baltimore neighbourhoods with drug and sex markets for the EMERALD cohort; all women enrolled in EMERALD from April 2018 to February 2019 were invited after their EMERALD visit (Methods 2 and 2.1, AM pp. 3–4). 52 of 175 approached declined screening, mostly for lack of time, childcare or withdrawal (Fig. 2, AM p. 16; Discussion, AM p. 10). Payment: $10 Visa gift card at baseline and $20 at follow-up (AM p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: EMERALD: aged 18 or over, self-identified cis-gender woman, sold or traded sex in the past 6 months, picked up clients 3 or more times in the past 3 months, willing to give contact details (AM p. 3). FIT: enrolled in EMERALD and used illegally obtained opioids (heroin, fentanyl or street-bought pills) in the past month (AM p. 4). All 20 ineligible women had not used opioids in the past month (Fig. 2, AM p. 16).
sample.demographics: Baseline, n = 103 (Table 1, AM pp. 17–18; Results, AM p. 6): 22.3% aged 18–29 and 54% under 40; 59.2% non-Hispanic White, 34.0% non-Hispanic Black, 6.8% Hispanic; 87.4% actively selling sex; 65.1% homeless in the past 6 months; 48.5% injected heroin and 30.1% injected fentanyl in the past 6 months; 73.8% smoked crack cocaine; 10.7% had ever used a strip; 75.7% concerned about fentanyl in their drugs and 42.7% preferring drugs with fentanyl; 96.1% used drugs alone.
sample.attrition: 68 of 103 (66%) completed follow-up, on average 56 days after baseline and 22.1% within the one-month target (AM p. 6; Fig. 2). Women aged 18–29 (34.3% of those lost versus 16.2% of completers, p = 0.04) and women who injected opioid pills (11.4% versus 1.5%, p = 0.03) were more often lost; no other baseline differences (AM p. 6; Table 1).
sample.selection_effects: A small convenience sample of women already in a cohort study, 70% of those approached agreeing to screening, analysed as completers only. The authors note the low participation rate may have caused selection bias (AM p. 10). Results apply to street-based women who sell sex and use opioids in one city with a fentanyl-dominated market.

exposure.measurement: The FIT bundle was given to everyone at baseline: 5 to 10 minutes of training in collecting a sample, testing and reading results; harm-reduction micro-counselling tailored to the risks reported in the baseline interview (for example on mixing alcohol and opioids, using alone, test doses, naloxone and polysubstance use); an insert card with strip instructions and overdose-prevention messages; five BTNX Rapid Response strips; injection equipment; and two doses of intramuscular naloxone (Methods 2.1, AM p. 4; Fig. 1, AM p. 15). Strip use, timing and results were self-reported at follow-up (Methods 2.2.3, AM p. 5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to drug doses. Five strips at baseline; more strips, injection equipment and naloxone offered at follow-up and at later cohort visits (AM p. 4).
exposure.polysubstance: Baseline past-6-month use (Table 1): smoked crack cocaine 73.8%, snorted or smoked heroin 62.1%, injected heroin 48.5%, snorted powdered cocaine 34.0%, benzodiazepine pills 21.4%; alcohol in the past month 43.7%. Benzodiazepine and alcohol use were outcomes; no adjustment.

comparison.controls: None: single-arm pretest–posttest. The 68 completers were stratified post hoc into women who used at least one strip (57) and women who used none (11) (Statistical analysis, AM p. 6; Table 3, AM p. 21).
comparison.matching: None; unadjusted McNemar tests within each group.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Without a comparison group, secular trends, regression to the mean after enrolment at a time of heavy use, and the effects of the counselling, naloxone and the cohort visit itself cannot be separated from strip use.

outcomes.instruments: Interviewer-administered computer-assisted surveys of about 10 minutes at baseline and follow-up (AM pp. 4–5): use of each drug by route, frequency dichotomized as daily or less; one AUDIT-C question on drinking frequency; agreement with preferring fentanyl and with concern about fentanyl (5-point scales); solitary use, asking someone to check on you and being near someone with naloxone (any versus never); non-fatal overdose to the point of passing out in the past month; mental health care, needle exchange and medication treatment; at follow-up, strips used, unused, lost or given away, timing of testing, results, surprise (with open-ended reasons), actions after positive and negative results (select all that apply) and likelihood of future use (AM pp. 5–6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study-specific items; only the drinking question comes from a validated instrument (AUDIT-C).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary prespecified outcome: number of non-fatal overdoses (AM p. 4), analysed as any versus none. Risk behaviours as prevalence or daily use; change as baseline versus follow-up proportions by McNemar's test (AM p. 6).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 15 rows in Table 3 plus any illicit opioid use reported in the text, each tested in the total sample and in two strata (about 45 McNemar tests), at p < 0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: interviews by study staff, and participants and staff knew everyone had received the intervention; whether the interviewers also delivered the training is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Only counts and percentages with significance stars; no odds ratios or confidence intervals are printed although the Methods say McNemar's test produced them (AM p. 6). Total sample, n = 68, baseline to follow-up (Table 3, AM p. 21): daily illicit opioid use 52 (76.5%) to 38 (55.9%), p < 0.01; daily injection 27 (39.7%) to 17 (25.0%), p < 0.01; benzodiazepine use 15 (22.1%) to 5 (7.4%), p < 0.01; daily benzodiazepine use 9 (13.2%) to 2 (2.9%), p < 0.05; solitary use 56 (94.9%) to 40 (67.8%), p < 0.001, among 59 with opioid use at follow-up; asking someone to check 36 (61.0%) to 43 (72.8%), not significant; non-fatal overdose 6 (8.8%) to 1 (1.5%), not significant; any injection 34 (50.0%) to 29 (42.7%), alcohol use 32 (47.1%) to 29 (42.7%) and preferring fentanyl 29 (42.7%) to 26 (38.2%), all not significant. The abstract gives p = 0.003, 0.004, 0.008 and < 0.001 for the first four of these (AM p. 1). Women who used no strip (n = 11): daily illicit opioid use 9 (81.8%) to 4 (36.4%), daily injection 4 (36.4%) to 2 (18.2%), non-fatal overdose 2 to 0, none significant. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% CI): used at least one strip 57/68 = 83.8% (73.3 to 90.7); harm-reduction behaviour after a positive result 33/48 = 68.8% (54.7 to 80.1); used the tested drugs after a positive result 30/48 = 62.5% (48.4 to 74.8); likely to use strips again 65/68 = 95.6% (87.8 to 98.5).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the number of non-fatal overdoses is described as the primary prespecified outcome (AM p. 4). Approved by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health IRB (AM p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports significant secondary outcomes and omits the primary outcome, which did not change significantly (6 to 1 women with an overdose). The Discussion calls overdose six times lower at follow-up while noting non-significance (AM p. 8). The text mixes figures from the total sample and from the strip-use stratum (AM p. 7).
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; the authors say the small sample and suboptimal retention may have left the analysis underpowered (AM p. 10).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In about two months, 57 of 68 followed-up women used at least one of five strips, 49 of them reported a positive result, and 65 of 68 said they were likely to use strips again. After a positive result 30 of 48 used the tested drugs (several to relieve withdrawal) and 33 of 48 reported at least one protective action, most often using a smaller amount (15) or going slower (10); after a negative result 21 of 24 used the drugs as intended. Daily opioid use, daily injection, benzodiazepine use and solitary use were lower at follow-up than at baseline, but the women who used no strip changed as much or more, there was no comparison group, and the baseline drug-use questions covered six months against one month at follow-up.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the study found reductions in drug use frequency and solitary drug use following strip use and that strip-based interventions hold potential for reducing overdose risk (AM p. 2); the Discussion calls the study a documentation of the short-term effectiveness of a brief strip intervention (AM p. 8). These causal readings rest on uncontrolled pre–post changes after a bundle whose counselling and insert card themselves advised against using alone and warned about mixing drugs such as alcohol and benzodiazepines with opioids; the women who used no strip also reduced daily opioid use (81.8% to 36.4%); the drug-use comparisons pair a six-month baseline window with a one-month follow-up window (AM p. 5); and the prespecified primary outcome is not in the abstract. The limitations paragraph acknowledges the lack of a control group, the single follow-up, low participation and social desirability (AM p. 10), and the authors call for a larger longitudinal study (AM p. 8).

timeline.event: Krieger et al. (2018): Rhode Island pilot in young adults, whose one-month follow-up this study copied for comparability (AM p. 4). This paper summarizes it as 87 people with 68% versus 32% behaviour change after positive results (AM p. 3); card sc_krieger_2018 records 81 analysed and 67.7% versus 12.9% (positive versus no positive result).
Karamouzian et al. (2018): low uptake of drug checking among clients of a Vancouver supervised injection facility, cited (card sc_karamouzian_2018).
Peiper et al. (2019): cross-sectional study of people who inject drugs, cited as finding five-fold odds of harm-reduction behaviour after a positive result; not read.
This pilot published (November issue; author manuscript in PubMed Central).

Gelberg et al. (2025): multi-state cohort of 541 people citing this study; most strip uses were followed by no change in amount, and negative results by more reports of using more (card sc_gelberg_2025).

replication.where_it_stands: No controlled replication of the pre–post changes appears in the sources read. The descriptive findings (uptake, frequent positive results, protective actions after positive results reported by a minority to a majority depending on the action, high acceptability) agree with other self-report studies of strips. The authors call for a larger longitudinal study (AM pp. 8, 10).

funding.funder: Supported in part by the National Institute on Drug Abuse (5R01DA041243-04) and the Johns Hopkins University Center for AIDS Research (1P30AI094189); Dr Park partly by a Center for AIDS Research Faculty Development Grant, C. Tomko in part by the National Institute of Mental Health (F31MH118817) and Dr Marshall in part by the National Institute of General Medical Sciences (P20GM125507); the funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis or interpretation (AM p. 11).
funding.declared_conflicts: SGS is an expert witness for plaintiffs in opioid litigation (Declaration of Competing Interest, AM p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health (Health, Behavior and Society) and Brown University (Epidemiology). The insert card carries the logo of SPARC, a centre for women in Baltimore (Fig. 1, AM p. 15). Recorded as context, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial among women who sell sex and use opioids (and other people who use drugs) in which both arms receive the same counselling and naloxone and only one receives strips, with the same recall periods at both time points, verified outcomes (urine toxicology, overdose records), and follow-up of several months.

domains.note: No comparison group: pre–post changes may reflect regression to the mean, secular change or the co-delivered counselling and insert card (which advised against using alone and warned about mixing drugs such as alcohol and benzodiazepines with opioids) and naloxone. The post hoc comparison of women who used strips with those who did not is unadjusted, and the 11 who used none changed as much or more.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: 70% of women approached agreed to screening; a cohort-based convenience sample; analysis restricted to the 66% who completed follow-up, with younger women and those injecting pills lost more often.
Everyone received the bundle; whether and how strips were used, and the results, were self-reported and unverified; 18% gave strips to others.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Follow-up took on average 56 days instead of one month (22.1% within the target), so exposure time varied; additional strips and naloxone were available at later cohort visits.
34% lost to follow-up, complete-case analysis; item non-response (for example 5 of 29 women with a negative result lacked answers on actions; 3 missing on surprise).

Self-reported to study staff who knew everyone had received the intervention (social desirability, recall; acknowledged, AM p. 10); unvalidated items; drug use at baseline asked for the past 6 months and at follow-up for the past month (AM p. 5), which by itself tends to produce apparent reductions.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: The prespecified primary outcome (number of non-fatal overdoses) was analysed only as any versus none and omitted from the abstract; about 45 unadjusted tests; odds ratios and intervals described in the Methods are not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I judges whether the study can estimate the effect of providing strips with training. It cannot: there is no comparison group, the intervention was a bundle with counselling that targeted the same behaviours, the women who used no strip changed as much or more, and the drug-use questions covered different periods before and after. Citable for: uptake (57 of 68 used at least one strip), self-reported results (49 of 57 with at least one positive), what women said they did after positive and negative results (for example 15 of 48 used a smaller amount after a positive result; 30 of 48 used the tested drugs; 21 of 24 used drugs as intended after a negative result), surprise at results, sharing of strips and acceptability, all as self-reports from 68 women in Baltimore in 2018–2019. Not citable for: strips reducing drug use, benzodiazepine use, solitary use or overdose.

key_findings.finding: Of 175 women approached, 123 were screened, 103 were eligible and enrolled (all ineligible women had not used opioids in the past month), and 68 (66%) completed follow-up, on average 56 days after baseline and 22.1% within the one-month target.
key_findings.note: The counts are in Fig. 2, an image, and were read from the rendered page; 103 enrolled and 68 followed up are also in the abstract (AM p. 1).

key_findings.finding: At baseline every woman received 5 to 10 minutes of strip training, harm-reduction micro-counselling tailored to the risks she reported, an insert card, five BTNX strips, injection equipment and two doses of intramuscular naloxone.

Baseline (n = 103): 22.3% aged 18–29, 59.2% non-Hispanic White, 87.4% actively selling sex, 48.5% injected heroin and 30.1% fentanyl in the past 6 months, 73.8% smoked crack cocaine, 10.7% had ever used a strip, 75.7% were concerned about fentanyl in their drugs, 42.7% preferred drugs with fentanyl and 96.1% used drugs alone.

At follow-up 57 of 68 (83.8%) had used at least one strip: 33 (57.9%) only before using drugs, 17 (29.8%) before and after, 7 (12.3%) only after. Of the 57, 49 (86.0%) had at least one positive result, 29 (50.9%) at least one negative and 8 (14.0%) an unclear result; 34 still had unused strips and 12 (17.7%) had given strips to others.

After a positive result (48 women with answers), 33 (68.8%) reported at least one harm-reduction behaviour and 30 (62.5%) used the tested drugs; 15 (31.3%) used a smaller amount than intended, 10 (20.8%) went slower when injecting, 5 (10.4%) did a tester shot, 3 (6.3%) asked someone to check on them, 3 (6.3%) threw the drugs out, 3 (6.3%) sold them, 6 (12.5%) told others and 2 (4.2%) stopped going to that dealer; none stopped using drugs or entered treatment.

Of the 30 women who used drugs as intended despite a positive result, 12 cited withdrawal (some also a missed or insufficient methadone dose); others said they enjoyed or wanted fentanyl, had a fentanyl habit, or doubted the result.
key_findings.note: The denominators printed for these reasons (5/12, 2/12, 4/12) do not fit the 30; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: After a negative result (24 women with answers), 21 (87.5%) used their drugs as intended, 2 reported a harm-reduction behaviour and 2 sold the drugs.

31 women (57.4%) were surprised by their results: 26 of 48 (54.2%) with a positive and 17 of 24 (70.8%) with a negative result; all 5 women with only negative results had assumed fentanyl was in all drugs.
49 of 68 women (72.1%) said they were extremely likely and 16 (23.5%) likely to use strips in future; by the editors' sum, 65 of 68 (95.6%).

Total sample (n = 68), baseline to follow-up: daily illicit opioid use 76.5% to 55.9%, daily injection 39.7% to 25.0% and benzodiazepine use 22.1% to 7.4% (each p < 0.01); solitary use 94.9% to 67.8% (p < 0.001; n = 59 with opioid use at follow-up); asking someone to check on you 61.0% to 72.8% and non-fatal overdose 8.8% to 1.5% (6 to 1 women), not significant; preference for fentanyl 42.7% to 38.2%, not significant.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (AM p. 1); Table 3, Total columns (AM p. 21)
key_findings.note: The baseline drug-use questions covered the past 6 months and the follow-up questions the past month (Methods 2.2.2, AM p. 5); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Women who used no strip (n = 11) changed in the same direction, some by more: daily illicit opioid use 81.8% to 36.4%, daily injection 36.4% to 18.2%, non-fatal overdose 2 to 0 women; none significant, which the authors attribute to the small group.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1, end (AM p. 8); Table 3, Did not use any FTS columns (AM p. 21)

key_findings.finding: The primary prespecified outcome was the number of non-fatal overdoses; it was analysed as any overdose in the past month (6 of 68 women at baseline, 1 at follow-up) and did not change significantly.
key_findings.locator: Methods 2, last sentence (AM p. 4); Results 3.1 (AM p. 8); Table 3 (AM p. 21)

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods state that drug use was asked for the past 6 months at baseline and the past month at follow-up, while Table 3 labels all drug-use rows as past month; the baseline values in Table 3 (benzodiazepine use 22.1%, any injection 50.0%) equal the past-6-month values for completers in Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pre–post reductions in drug use compare a six-month window with a one-month window, which by itself produces lower follow-up figures; they cannot be read as changes in behaviour.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives solitary drug use as 96% versus 68%; Table 3 gives 94.9% versus 67.8% (96.1% is the baseline of all 103 women). The abstract's 24% who had overdosed in the past year appears nowhere in the body, where Table 1 gives 9.7% with a non-fatal overdose.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract mixes denominators and contains a figure that cannot be checked; cite the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text gives benzodiazepine use among women who used strips as 22.8% to 7.40%; Table 3 gives 22.8% to 7.0% for that group, and 7.4% is the total sample's follow-up value. Non-significant changes are referred to Table 2 instead of Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; figures from different groups are combined in one sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: Denominators in the Results text do not match Table 2: 25 women with a negative result in the text against 24 with answers (29 with a negative result, 5 missing) in Table 2, with percentages (87.5%, 8.3%) that fit 24; reasons for using drugs despite a positive result given as 5/12, 2/12 and 4/12 for a group of 30; and 24/25 (96%) likely to use strips again against 49 extremely likely and 16 likely out of 68 in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentages are usable from Table 2, but the open-ended reasons cannot be quantified reliably.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 30 of 48 women used their drugs as originally intended, without behavioural modifications, after a positive result, while Table 2 shows 33 of 48 engaged in a harm-reduction behaviour; in a select-all question at least 15 women must have done both.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text's gloss of used the tested drugs as no behavioural modification is not consistent with the table; the categories overlap and should not be added.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say McNemar's test produced odds ratios and confidence intervals, and the Results say these show the precision of the estimates, but no table or text reports them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of the pre–post changes cannot be judged from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The strip validation figures of 98% sensitivity and 94% specificity are attributed to Sherman et al. (2018) in the Introduction and to Krieger et al. (2018) in the Discussion; baseline concern about fentanyl among completers is 80.9% in Table 1 but 83.8% in Table 3.

No supplementary material is mentioned.
